title: A Review of the Gut Microbiota as a Regulator of Muscle Quality and Flavor in Farmed Fish
content: As aquaculture shifts focus from yield to edible product attributes, muscle quality (encompassing texture, nutritional composition, and oxidative stability) alongside ﬂavor proﬁles collectively determine consumer acceptance and economic value. Emerging evidence indicates that the gut microbiota, operating through the microbiota–gut–muscle axis, can regulate nutrient absorption, lipid and amino acid metabolism, extracellular matrix deposition, and the synthesis of ﬂavor-active metabolites. This review synthesizes research spanning the two decades from the ﬁrst gnotobiotic zebraﬁsh experiments to the present, integrating gnotobiotic models, 16S rRNA surveys, metagenomics, transcriptomics, and metabolomics, alongside dietary interventions in commercially important species. The conceptual trajectory is traced from early host-microbiota interdependence in zebraﬁsh to recent causal demonstrations that speciﬁc bacteria and their metabolites alter muscle collagen synthesis and ﬂesh ﬂavor. Evidence linking microbiota composition to muscle texture, taste-active compounds, volatile aromas, and geosmin/2-methylisoborneol related oﬀ-ﬂavors is critically evaluated, while modulation strategies including probiotics, prebiotics, and RAS management are assessed. Finally, critical knowledge gaps, notably the scarcity of causal evidence and neglect of host sex and genetics, are identiﬁed, and precision modulation framework is proposed. This framework matches microbiome-informed interventions to speciﬁc species, life stages, and production systems and is designed to guide interventions aimed at improving ﬁsh muscle quality and ﬂavor, with eﬀectiveness to be validated experimentally.
